archetype.name: Retooling (run-first, pass-broken)
archetype.definition: A team with a legitimate ground game and one of the league's cleanest pockets whose passing attack and ball security sink it. The rest of the year is about finding out whether Michael Penix Jr. can turn that foundation into points.

report.headline: A real run game and clean pocket, wasted by a broken passing attack
report.take:
Atlanta at 3-7 is not unlucky so much as lopsided. The point differential of -57 implies about 3.9 wins, so the record roughly matches the play. The zero in one-score games stings, but the losses have mostly been decisive. The roster has two things that work. Bijan Robinson drives a rushing offense that ranks 8th in EPA per carry and 5th in yards per carry. The line allows pressure at the 2nd-lowest rate in the league and QB hits at the lowest. That is a better base than most 3-7 teams have.

The problem is everything that happens once the ball leaves the quarterback's hand. Passing EPA ranks 30th, and the offense has given the ball away 19 times against 10 takeaways. Because the pocket is clean, the line is not the excuse. The breakdowns come from decisions, accuracy and what the receivers do with the ball. The season split early: Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa started the first two games, and the 3-34 loss to Carolina had five giveaways. Penix has started every game since. His era opened with two convincing wins in which the offense ran for 242 and 205 yards. Then came the tell: a 16-0 shutout in Tampa with four turnovers and -19.3 passing EPA, followed by double-digit losses to Cincinnati and Kansas City.

The rest of the team is average, and that is not enough to cover for the offense. The defense ranks 14th in EPA allowed and gets home for QB hits (6th in hit rate). It is soft on third down (24th) and gives up explosive runs at the 2nd-worst rate in the league; Tampa ran for 324 yards with zero passing yards. Special teams rank 29th in EPA per game, a hidden tax in close games. History says none of this is new. This franchise has won between 4 and 8 games every year since 2018, usually with negative wins over expected and poor ATS marks. Under Stefanski it is the same mid-pack-to-below team, now with a quarterback still proving he can carry the passing half.

strengths.title: A rushing attack that travels
strengths.body: Atlanta's run game is efficient, not just a product of game script: 8th in rush EPA, 5th in yards per carry and 5th in stuff rate. The blockers aren't opening huge lanes (25th in yards before contact), so a lot of this is Robinson making yards on his own across 185 carries. It should hold as long as he stays healthy and the offense isn't forced to abandon it by early deficits.

strengths.title: Pass protection among the league's best
strengths.body: The line allows pressure on 14% of dropbacks (2nd) and the lowest QB hit rate in football. That is a real, repeatable trait and it takes the usual excuse away from the passing game. It also gives Penix a stable platform to develop on for the rest of the year.

strengths.title: A pass rush that hits quarterbacks
strengths.body: The defense ranks 10th in pressure rate and 6th in QB hit rate, so it can disrupt bad lines. Those hits haven't turned into sacks often enough (21st in sack rate), which caps the payoff. Even so, it is the defense's best weapon against a shaky protection unit.

concerns.title: Passing game and giveaways
concerns.body: Passing EPA ranks 30th despite elite protection, and 19 turnovers have produced a -9 turnover differential. Some of that is the Tagovailoa disaster against Carolina. But the Tampa shutout and the Kansas City loss came under Penix, so this is the core flaw, not noise. Until it improves, the run game keeps getting erased by one or two possessions.

concerns.title: Special teams bleeding field position
concerns.body: At -2.98 EPA per game, the third phase ranks 29th. That is points handed away every week, and it matters most in exactly the one-score games Atlanta has failed to win. Nothing in the dossier suggests a fix is coming.

concerns.title: Defense leaks chunk runs and third downs
concerns.body: The per-play numbers are average, but the defense allows explosive runs at the 2nd-worst rate and ranks 24th on third down. Those two leaks extend drives and flip games. Tampa's 324 rushing yards was the extreme version. It is a structural flaw in run fits and tackling that offenses with any ground game will test.

trend.note: Penix's first two starts were the season's best football, and the upset of San Francisco looked like a turn. Since then Atlanta has lost three straight by double digits: shut out in Tampa, then routed by Cincinnati and Kansas City with the passing game negative in all three.

nextGame.headline: Atlanta's clean pocket meets the league's most ferocious pass rush
nextGame.body:
Minnesota is the inverse of Atlanta. The Vikings own the league's best defense by EPA, allow the fewest points, lead the league in pressure rate and red-zone defense, and rank 1st on special teams. The offense is bad: 30th in play-by-play EPA, with a run game 27th in EPA and a sack rate allowed of 9%. Their 7-3 record also carries some luck: 2.12 wins over expected. Offenses run against this defense far more than usual (the league's strongest run funnel), and its explosive-run rate allowed ranks only 24th. That points Atlanta at Robinson. The Book makes Minnesota a 7-point favorite with a 42.5 total, which reads as a grinding, low-scoring game Atlanta has to keep close.

Availability tilts slightly toward Atlanta. Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring strain, so Kirk Cousins, who started the last two games, runs a weak offense without Jordan Addison, a 92%-snap receiver out after thumb surgery. Minnesota is also without corner Isaiah Rodgers, an 83%-snap starter. Atlanta comes off a bye with 14 days of rest but is listed without linebacker Divine Deablo, a 78%-snap regular, and backup receiver Zachariah Branch.

waysToWin.title: Feed Robinson into the run funnel
waysToWin.body: Minnesota's defense is strongest against the pass, and offenses lean on the run against it more than against anyone else. Atlanta's 8th-ranked rush offense can stay ahead of the chains and keep Penix out of obvious passing downs. Long, run-heavy drives also shorten a game Atlanta needs to keep low-scoring.

waysToWin.title: Harass Cousins behind a leaky line
waysToWin.body: Minnesota allows sacks at the 5th-worst rate and is down its top receiver and its preferred quarterback. Atlanta's pass rush ranks 6th in QB hit rate. If it finishes a few of those hits, the Vikings' 28th-ranked offense may not reach 20 points.

waysToWin.title: Protection wins the marquee matchup
waysToWin.body: Atlanta's line ranks 2nd in pressure rate allowed and Minnesota's rush ranks 1st in pressure rate. If the line holds that standard, Penix gets clean looks against a secondary missing a starting corner. Opposing WR1s have also produced per-play efficiency against this defense, so there is room for Drake London.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers hand Minnesota short fields
waysToLose.body: Minnesota wins the turnover battle at the 2nd-best rate, while Atlanta's offense has already given it away 19 times. The Vikings' offense can't sustain drives on its own, so giveaways are its likeliest route to points. Two Penix mistakes probably decide this game.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone trips end in field goals
waysToLose.body: Minnesota allows touchdowns on just 25% of red-zone trips, the best rate in the league. Atlanta's passing game is 30th in EPA and the least equipped to finish in tight spaces. Moving the ball on the ground but settling for threes keeps the Vikings comfortably ahead of a 7-point line.

waysToLose.title: The special teams gap swings it
waysToLose.body: This is the league's best special teams unit against one of its worst. In a game with a 42.5 total, a big return, a blocked kick or consistently worse field position does the work Minnesota's offense can't. It is the quietest way for Atlanta to lose a game it otherwise keeps close.

nextGame.watch: Atlanta's early-down run success: if Robinson keeps the offense out of third-and-long, the league's top pass rush is neutralized; if not, Penix is throwing into it.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is real and should last: the run game, the protection and a pass rush that hits quarterbacks are traits, not streaks. What should ease a little is the turnover differential, since one five-giveaway game under a since-benched starter inflates it. Even so, Penix has had multi-turnover games of his own, and this franchise's turnover numbers have run negative most years, so don't expect a swing to the plus side. Special teams look like a fixed cost. The record already reflects the point differential, so there is no hidden bounce coming from luck.

The schedule offers chances. Detroit's defense ranks 27th, and New Orleans, Washington and Carolina are all middling. A weak NFC South leaves Atlanta technically alive behind 5-5 Carolina, with three division games still to play. Tampa's 3rd-ranked defense already shut this offense out, though, and the passing game hasn't shown it can win shootouts. The likeliest finish is a handful more wins, landing in the same mid-single-digit range this franchise keeps visiting. That makes the rest of the season mostly an audition for Penix.
swingFactors: Results in the three division games

confidence.note: Ten games with a clear Penix-era sample, but early QB churn and a few blowouts skew the totals.
